chapter_title: Interacting with Smart Contracts from the Frontend (Writing Data & Transactions)

screens.title: Writing Data: Sending Transactions from the Frontend
screens.subtitle: How your dApp creates state changes on-chain using signed transactions, feedback, and error handling

narration.text: In this lesson you'll learn how a dApp sends transactions that change contract state. Writing to a smart contract requires a cryptographically signed transaction from the user's account, which consumes gas and takes time to be mined. We'll use the Greeter contract's setGreeting example to show the full flow: obtaining a signer, instantiating the contract for writing, prompting the wallet, awaiting confirmation with tx. wait, and handling errors like reverts or insufficient funds. You will also see how payable functions accept Ether and how to pass value when calling them. Practically, this matters because read-only calls are immediate and free, but write operations are UX-sensitive — they can fail, incur fees, and need clear progress states. By the end you will understand why a signer is required, how to interpret a TransactionReceipt, common user-facing failure modes, and what feedback to show your users so they aren't left wondering what happened. Think about a user clicking "confirm" in their wallet: your app must guide them before, during, and after that confirmation so state stays consistent and errors are actionable.

keyIdea.title: Core idea
keyIdea.text: Transactions require a signer and gas; use tx.wait() to confirm success and offer clear UX for pending, confirmed, and failed states.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: Skills you will gain in this chapter

narration.text: By the end of this chapter you will be able to distinguish between read-only calls and transactions, create frontend logic to send state-changing calls, and manage the full transaction lifecycle. You will implement a write operation that uses a signer to sign and broadcast a transaction, and you will wait for a TransactionReceipt to confirm success. You will also learn to send Ether with payable functions by providing a value override in the transaction call. These skills matter because writing to the chain is fundamentally different from reading: it costs gas, can revert, and requires explicit user authorization. A concrete example is updating the Greeter contract's greeting: you will add new state, prompt the wallet to sign, and refresh the UI after the tx is mined. Finally, you will practice parsing errors such as user rejection or revert messages so your UI can present clear, actionable feedback. This reduces user frustration and prevents repeated failed attempts.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Implementation & UX
screens.subtitle: Practical tasks and the user experience you will build

narration.text: These objectives focus on hands-on implementation and user-facing behavior. You will add state variables like newGreeting, transactionStatus, and isMining to your frontend state, and wire them into a function that sends a write transaction to the Greeter contract. You will practice disabling inputs while mining, showing a transaction hash when the tx is broadcast, and refreshing contract state after confirmation. You should also be able to call payable functions by passing a value override and convert human readable Ether to Wei before sending. Finally, you will learn to detect common pitfalls: calling a write method when only a provider exists, insufficient funds for gas, network mismatches, and transaction reverts because of require statements. Each objective is grounded in a concrete change you can test locally with a wallet like MetaMask connected to a test network. Practicing these will make your dApp robust and user friendly during real transactions.

screens.title: What is a Transaction?
screens.subtitle: Definition, properties, and why transactions differ from view calls

narration.text: A transaction is a cryptographically signed instruction that is broadcast to the blockchain network and can modify contract state or transfer assets. Unlike view or pure calls, which only read state and return data immediately, transactions consume gas, can be mined in a later block, and either succeed or revert based on contract logic. A concrete example is calling setGreeting on the Greeter contract: that call changes the greeting variable and therefore requires a transaction. When your frontend calls a write method, the wallet prompts the user to sign; the call returns a TransactionResponse with a hash, and then you call tx. wait() to obtain the TransactionReceipt once mining completes. A common misconception is to expect transactions to behave like synchronous function calls — they do not. State updates from transactions are not instant, can be reordered by miners, and may fail if gas is insufficient or a require() check fails. Key takeaway: treat transactions as asynchronous, costly operations that need explicit user consent, careful error parsing, and post-confirmation state refreshes to keep UI consistent. How will you reflect that asynchronous cost in your user experience?

keyIdea.title: Transaction essentials
keyIdea.text: Signed, gas-consuming, asynchronous operations that change state and require explicit handling in the frontend.

content.html:
Core Concept

What is a Transaction?

A brief definition and the properties that distinguish transactions from read-only calls.

Signed by a user and broadcast to the network.
Consumes gas and can transfer Ether when payable.
Asynchronous: returns a tx hash, then is mined later.
Can revert due to require() or require-like checks; gas is still consumed.
Key Takeaway

Treat writes as non-instant operations and design your UI to handle pending, success, and failure states.

Example
// send transaction to set greeting
const tx = await greeterContract.setGreeting(newGreeting);
console.log('Hash:', tx.hash);
const receipt = await tx.wait();
if (receipt.status === 1) {
  // success: refresh state
}
Common misconception

Expecting immediate state changes after sending the transaction. The transaction must be mined and confirmed before UI state is authoritative.

screens.title: Signer vs Provider: Who signs the transaction?
screens.subtitle: Why a Signer is mandatory for write operations and how to instantiate a contract with it

narration.text: A Provider gives you access to read data and the network; a Signer represents a user account capable of authorizing and signing transactions. When your frontend only has a provider, contract instances can perform read-only work. To send a transaction you must supply a signer when you instantiate ethers. Contract so the library can create signed transactions and prompt the user's wallet. In practice that means detecting window. ethereum, creating a BrowserProvider, requesting account access, then obtaining a signer object tied to the connected account. A concrete example from the Greeter app: when both provider and signer exist you create the contract with the signer and assign it to greeterContract. If you forget to use a signer and call a write function, ethers. js will error because gas estimation requires signer context. A common misconception is that the provider can sign on behalf of the user — it cannot. The key takeaway is to gate write UI on the presence of a signer and to surface a clear error when one is absent. Always re-instantiate contract instances when the signer or account changes so permissions remain correct.

keyIdea.title: Signer requirement
keyIdea.text: Use a Signer for write operations; a Provider alone only supports read calls and cannot sign transactions.

content.html:
Process Flow

Signer vs Provider

Provider: read-only access to the network and state.
Signer: signs transactions and represents a user's account.
When signer is present, instantiate contract with signer to enable writes.
Misconception

A provider cannot sign; never assume read permission implies write permission.

Code pattern
// use signer when available
if (provider && signer) {
  const contract = new ethers.Contract(GREETER_CONTRACT_ADDRESS, GreeterABI.abi, signer);
  setGreeterContract(contract);
} else if (provider) {
  const contract = new ethers.Contract(GREETER_CONTRACT_ADDRESS, GreeterABI.abi, provider);
  setGreeterContract(contract);
}
Example consequence

Calling setGreeting without a signer triggers an error indicating a signer is required for gas estimation or signing.

screens.title: Implementing setGreeting in the Frontend
screens.subtitle: State variables, the handler function, and the transaction lifecycle code

narration.text: Implementing a write operation from the frontend requires three pieces of state and a handler function that orchestrates sending the transaction and waiting for its confirmation. Typical state includes newGreeting for user input, transactionStatus for feedback messages, and isMining to disable inputs while the operation is in-flight. The handler starts by validating inputs and presence of greeterContract and signer. It then calls greeterContract. setGreeting(newGreeting), which returns a TransactionResponse with a hash. Immediately present the hash to the user so they can inspect it in a block explorer if desired, and set a pending status. Next, call tx. wait() to pause until the transaction is mined; once you receive a TransactionReceipt, check receipt. status === 1 to confirm success. On success, clear inputs and re-fetch contract state so the displayed greeting updates. In the catch block, distinguish between user rejection (error code 4001) and on-chain reverts that include an error message. This function needs to set isMining true at the start and false in finally so the UI always reflects the correct enabled state. A common mistake is not awaiting tx. wait(), which leads to stale UI if the user expects immediate confirmation.

keyIdea.title: Handler pattern
keyIdea.text: Validate input, send tx, show hash, await tx.wait(), refresh state on success, and always clear mining flag in finally.

content.html:
Definition

Front-end handler structure

  • Input validation and signer check.
  • Send transaction and capture tx.hash immediately.
  • Await tx.wait() for TransactionReceipt and check receipt.status.
  • Update UI and refetch contract state on success.
  • Parse errors and ensure isMining is reset in finally.
Takeaway

A clear lifecycle in code leads to unambiguous UX during async writes.

Code Walkthrough
const handleSetGreeting = async () => {
  if (!greeterContract || !signer) { setError('Wallet not connected'); return; }
  if (!newGreeting.trim()) { setError('Greeting cannot be empty'); return; }
  try {
    setIsMining(true);
    setTransactionStatus('Sending transaction...');
    const tx = await greeterContract.setGreeting(newGreeting);
    setTransactionStatus(`Transaction sent: ${tx.hash}. Waiting for confirmation...`);
    const receipt = await tx.wait();
    if (receipt.status === 1) { setTransactionStatus('Transaction confirmed successfully!'); await fetchContractData(greeterContract); }
    else { setTransactionStatus('Transaction failed!'); setError('Transaction failed on chain.'); }
  } catch (err) { /* parse error codes and messages */ }
  finally { setIsMining(false); }
};
Note: do not forget to clear the input and refresh state after a confirmed transaction so the user sees the updated greeting.

screens.title: Transaction Lifecycle: send → pending → mined
screens.subtitle: How to surface transaction hash, pending state, and confirmation to users

narration.text: When a user triggers a write action, the frontend should present three clear states: sent, pending, and final (confirmed or failed). First, sending the transaction returns a TransactionResponse with a hash; show that hash and set the status to sent so users know their wallet processed the request. Next, while waiting for confirmation, present a pending state and disable the relevant inputs to prevent duplicate submissions. Use tx. wait() to block until the transaction is mined. When the receipt arrives, check receipt. status: a value of 1 indicates success and you should refresh contract data and present a success message; any other status indicates a failure on chain and should be surfaced as an error. Also log gasUsed and blockNumber from the receipt for debugging and optional display. A common UX mistake is failing to disable inputs or not showing the transaction hash, which leaves users uncertain whether their action went through. Another pitfall is treating the broadcasted hash as final; networks can drop transactions before mining. The takeaway: make the lifecycle explicit in your UI and guide users through each step so they can trust what happened.

keyIdea.title: Lifecycle
keyIdea.text: Show hash immediately, present a pending state, await tx.wait(), then check receipt.status and refresh state accordingly.

content.html:
Process Flow

Transaction lifecycle

Sent

Show tx.hash immediately after the wallet signs and broadcasts the transaction so users can inspect it externally.

Pending

Disable inputs, show a spinner or message, and explain that the network is processing the transaction.

Mined / Final

Check receipt.status. On success, refresh data; on failure, parse revert and guide the user.

Example

After greeterContract.setGreeting(newGreeting), show the hash and then await tx.wait() to update the greeting displayed.

Common mistake

Assuming a broadcasted hash equals success before the transaction is mined.

screens.title: Payable functions and sending Ether
screens.subtitle: How to call payable contract functions and include value from the frontend

narration.text: Payable functions accept Ether alongside a state change. To call them from the frontend, include an overrides object with a value field in Wei. Convert human-readable Ether like '0.01' using a helper, then pass that value when calling the contract method. A concrete example is the Greeter. deposit() function: you call greeterContract. deposit({ value: ethers. parseEther(amountInEther) }) and then await tx. wait() as with any write. Remember that payable functions still consume gas, and the value sent will be transferred into the contract if the call succeeds. A common misconception is thinking that sending Ether with a write is free; it still costs gas on top of the transferred amount. Another pitfall is forgetting to convert Ether to Wei, causing incorrect or failed transactions. The takeaway: always validate the amount, convert it correctly before sending, and ensure the signer has sufficient balance to cover both the value and the gas fees. Inform users of both the amount they send and the expected gas cost so they approve with full awareness. Payable functions and sending Ether means use an overrides object with value in wei; convert ether strings to wei and ensure funds cover both value and gas.. In practical terms, how to call payable contract functions and include value from the frontend. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Payable calls
keyIdea.text: Use an overrides object with value in Wei; convert Ether strings to Wei and ensure funds cover both value and gas.

content.html:
Definition

Payable functions

Functions declared payable accept Ether; include a value override when calling from the frontend.

Convert Ether to Wei using parseEther before sending.
Ensure the signer has enough balance for value + gas.
Await tx.wait() to confirm the transfer succeeded on-chain.
Code snippet
const amountInEther = '0.01';
const tx = await greeterContract.deposit({ value: ethers.parseEther(amountInEther) });
await tx.wait();
Take care to surface both the value being sent and estimated gas to the user before they confirm in their wallet.

screens.title: Gas & Estimation: defaults and overrides
screens.subtitle: How gas affects transactions and when to override estimates

narration.text: Gas is the unit of computational work on Ethereum and paying for it in Ether is required for any state-changing operation. Ethers. js usually estimates gas automatically, but estimates can be incorrect for complex contracts or when external conditions change. If gas is set too low, the transaction may run out of gas and fail; if set too high, users may pay more than necessary. In your frontend, rely on automatic estimation in the common case, but provide optional fields for advanced users to set gasLimit or gasPrice if they understand the implications. Always catch errors caused by failed gas estimation and present a clear explanation and a retry path. A typical example is a contract function that performs more computation depending on input size — its gas cost can vary widely, so conservative estimates or dynamic inspection may be necessary. A common misconception is that gas is only about speed; while gas price affects miner incentives, gas limit controls resource allowances and failing to set it correctly causes a revert. The key takeaway is to trust automatic estimates but design for clear error messaging and safe user overrides for advanced scenarios.

keyIdea.title: Gas management
keyIdea.text: Trust automatic estimates for most cases; expose safe overrides for advanced users and handle out-of-gas errors gracefully.

content.html:
Comparison

Gas: automatic estimate vs manual override

Automatic estimation

Ethers.js estimates gas for common calls. Use this by default to simplify UX and reduce errors for typical users.

Best for most users
Manual override

Allow advanced users to set gasLimit or gasPrice when deterministic needs demand it. Validate inputs and explain risks.

Advanced option
Example

If a function loops over user input, gas can spike; warn and estimate higher for safety.

Common mistake

Setting gas too low and failing to surface the resulting revert meaningfully to the user.

screens.title: Transaction Reverts and Error Handling
screens.subtitle: Detecting user rejection, revert messages, and how to present actionable feedback

narration.text: Transactions can fail for multiple reasons: the user rejects the signature in their wallet, the transaction reverts on-chain due to a require() or revert(), or there are insufficient funds for gas. A robust try-catch block should distinguish these cases so your UI can give actionable messages. For example, user rejection is often indicated by an error code of 4001; in that case, show a polite message explaining the user cancelled. For on-chain reverts, some providers surface err. data. message which you can surface after sanitizing. If neither is available, present a general 'Transaction failed' with a suggestion to check their balance and the contract's requirements. Always set isMining back to false in finally so the UI remains responsive. A common misconception is to assume all errors are user cancellations; parsing the error structure helps reveal true reverts. The takeaway: parse errors conservatively, provide helpful next steps, and log detailed information for debugging without exposing raw error objects to end users. Transaction Reverts and Error Handling means differentiate user rejection, revert reasons, and insufficient funds; always reset mining state and present clear next steps.. In practical terms, detecting user rejection, revert messages, and how to present actionable feedback. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Error parsing
keyIdea.text: Differentiate user rejection, revert reasons, and insufficient funds; always reset mining state and present clear next steps.

content.html:
Definition

Transaction reverts & handling

User rejection

Detected via a wallet error code (e.g., 4001). Tell the user they cancelled and how to retry.

On-chain revert

Parse err.data.message when available and explain which require() likely failed or suggest contract rules to check.

Insufficient funds

Explain that gas+value exceed their balance and provide steps to add funds or reduce the value sent.

Pro tip

Log full error objects for debugging, but show cleaned user-friendly messages in the UI.

screens.title: UX Patterns: Pending, Success, Failure
screens.subtitle: Design states, disable controls, and refresh contract data after confirmation

narration.text: Transaction UX is critical. Users expect clear feedback while the network processes their action. Implement three UI states: pending (isMining true), success, and failure. When pending, disable the input and action controls, present a clear message like 'Transaction sent' with the tx hash, and optionally show an external explorer link. After receipt confirms success, refresh the contract data so read displays reflect the new state. If the transaction fails, show a readable explanation and suggest corrective actions such as checking balance or retrying with more gas. Avoid ambiguous states like a spinner without context. Also account for race conditions: if multiple users submit writes, the order of transactions is not guaranteed; design your contract and frontend to be tolerant to reordered events. A common mistake is relying solely on optimistic UI updates prior to confirmation; always reconcile the optimistic state with the on-chain state after the receipt. The takeaway is to lead the user confidently through the asynchronous process with explicit states and clear instructions on next steps. UX Patterns: Pending, Success, Failure means disable controls while mining, show the tx hash, refresh state on success, and present clear corrective guidance on failure.. In practical terms, design states, disable controls, and refresh contract data after confirmation. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: UX pattern
keyIdea.text: Disable controls while mining, show the tx hash, refresh state on success, and present clear corrective guidance on failure.

content.html:
Process Flow

UX Patterns for Transactions

Pending

Disable inputs and show tx.hash and an estimated wait message.

Success

Refresh contract data and show confirmation with block number for transparency.

Failure

Show a clear error, suggest checking balance or trying again, and log details for debugging.

Check your understanding

If you show an optimistic update, what step must you still perform to guarantee correctness? (Hint: reconcile with on-chain state after tx.wait.)

screens.title: Common Issues: Network mismatch, no signer, and race conditions
screens.subtitle: How these problems manifest and how to mitigate them in your dApp

narration.text: Three recurrent issues appear when sending transactions: the user's wallet is on a different network than your contract, the frontend lacks a signer and attempts a write, and race conditions from concurrent transactions change expected results. Network mismatch leads to failed calls or transactions to unknown addresses — detect the network chain ID and prompt users to switch before allowing writes. Attempting writes without a signer results in errors from ethers. js because gas estimation and signing are not possible — gate write buttons and show an explanatory message. Race conditions occur when multiple actors submit transactions affecting the same state; to mitigate them, design contracts defensively with checks and the frontend should handle out-of-order confirmations by re-fetching authoritative state after every confirmation. A practical mitigation for network mismatch is to check provider. getNetwork() and compare it to the contract's deployment network before enabling the write path. For no signer, prompt connection flow and do not attempt setGreeting until connected. The takeaway: proactively check environment and permissions to reduce avoidable failures and user confusion. Common Issues: Network mismatch, no signer, and race conditions means check network and signer presence, design contracts for concurrency, and always refresh authoritative state after transactions.. In practical terms, how these problems manifest and how to mitigate them in your dapp. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Mitigations
keyIdea.text: Check network and signer presence, design contracts for concurrency, and always refresh authoritative state after transactions.

content.html:
Common Mistake

Network, Signer, Race Conditions

Network mismatch

Check chain ID and require the correct network before enabling write actions.

No signer

Only instantiate write-capable contracts when a signer is present. Otherwise, present a connect flow.

Race conditions

Reconcile UI after every confirmation and design contracts to handle reordered operations safely.

Actionable check

Before enabling a write, verify the signer exists and network matches the deployment; otherwise, disable the button and explain how to proceed.

narration.text: Keep these concise concepts in mind as you build write-capable dApps. A transaction is a signed instruction that changes state and consumes gas. Nonpayable functions change state without accepting Ether; payable functions do accept Ether and require a value override. A Signer is required to sign and send transactions — a Provider alone supports only reads. tx. wait() blocks until a transaction is mined and returns a TransactionReceipt which shows success via receipt. status. Gas must be estimated and can be overridden, but incorrect gas limits cause failures. Transaction reverts consume gas and should be parsed and presented to users in friendly language. Use these points as a checklist when implementing transaction flows and designing the user experience. Signer
Represents a connected account that can sign and send transactions.
tx.wait()

Summary

Practically, these steps prevent common errors such as insufficient funds or calling a write with only a provider. When you test, deploy to a testnet and update the frontend address, then simulate failures to ensure your error parsing and user messages are helpful. These small checks make a big difference in user trust and dApp reliability.
